abstract: Juvenile fibromyalgia (JFM) is a chronic pain condition marked by widespread musculoskeletal pain and often accompanied by physical fatigue, nonrestorative sleep, headaches, anxiety, and depression. Previous studies have found that adolescents with fibromyalgia report augmented unpleasantness and altered brain responses to non-painful multisensory stimuli. Likewise, research in major depression has shown altered neural processing of sensory stimulation. We examined whether augmented brain responses to non-painful multisensory stimulation is associated with depressive symptoms in adolescent girls with JFM. Forty-six female adolescents with JFM (mean - SD, 16.43 - 1.10 years [range 13-18 years]) and 44 healthy participants (mean - SD, 16.09 - 1.06 years [range 13-18 years]) completed validated questionnaires assessing daily-life sensory hypersensitivity and depressive symptoms, alongside undergoing a functional MRI multisensory task. JFM patients reported significantly higher sensory unpleasantness than healthy participants, and this hypersensitivity was positively associated with depressive symptoms. Neuroimaging results in chronic pain patients revealed that greater depressive symptomatology was associated with increased activation in the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) (pFWE<0.05), a region implicated in self-referential processing and specifically rumination in adults with chronic pain. JFM patients showed increased PCC-left middle temporal gyrus task-dependent connectivity using psychophysiological interactions analysis (PPI). Furthermore, hyperconnectivity between the PCC and brain areas involved in cognitive-affective regulation, sensory integration, and memory processing was strongly correlated with depressive symptoms in JFM patients. These findings underscore the role of depressive symptoms in sensory processing and integration in JFM patients and highlight the complex interplay between sensory processing and emotional/self-referential brain function in patients.
